appraisal_events.evidence: j'avais retenu le nom de Balbec que nous avait cité Legrandin... « on y sent la véritable fin de la terre française, européenne, de la Terre antique »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator preserves and quotes at length Legrandin's evocative description of Balbec's coast, treating his words as a source that shaped his imaginative attachment to the place, paralleling (but quieter than) the admiration later given to Swann.

status_effects.explanation: Legrandin is granted local authority as the source of a memorable, poetically charged image of Balbec that lodges in the narrator's imagination.

ambiguities: Legrandin's grandiose, lyrical phrasing ('la véritable fin de la terre...') is consistent with his broader characterization elsewhere in the novel as pretentiously eloquent; within this passage alone there is no explicit ironic marker, but the admiration attributed to the narrator is more implicit and muted than the explicit appreciation given to Swann, so the endorsed reading is held with only moderate confidence.
Françoise's brief appearance (warning about storms, 'parlait en gémissant') is characterizing color rather than a socially positioned event and was judged too peripheral to score.

Le narrateur is present throughout as the remembering/perceiving consciousness and as Swann's interlocutor, but the passage stages him as an essayistic, reflective 'I' rather than a social participant being included, excluded, favored, or dismissed, so he was not scored per the supplement instructions.
